BY THE COURT :-
1.

By filing the present Civil Second Appeal, the appellants have questioned the legality and correctness of the judgment and decree dated 18.03.2025 passed by the learned Additional District Judge No.4, Jodhpur (Metropolitan) in Regular Civil Appeal No. 06/2025, affirming the order dated 17.12.2024 passed by the learned Additional Civil Judge No.3, Jodhpur Metropolitan in Civil Suit No.153/2022 whereby the plaint was rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.
2. Briefly stating the facts of the case are that the appellants- plaintiffs instituted a civil suit seeking permanent and mandatory injunction against the respondent-defendant, praying that the respondent be restrained from alienating Plot Nos. F-292 and E-1- 435 situated in the proposed RIICO Industrial Area, Kharabera, which were allotted in lieu of acquisition of land comprised in Khasra Nos. 384 and 385 of Village Kharabera, Tehsil Luni.
2.1 A further prayer was made for issuance of a direction to RIICO for execution of the lease deed in favour of the plaintiffs.

The suit,
registered on 09.11.2022, progressed after service upon the defendants on 19.11.2022.
On the same day, the learned Trial Court declined the prayer for temporary injunction without assigning any cogent reasons.

The appeal preferred under Order 43 Rule 1 CPC was dismissed on 31.01.2023,
leading to Writ Petition No. 2771/2023, wherein this Court directed consideration of the injunction application afresh while maintaining status quo.

Subsequently, the Trial Court allowed the application under Order (Uploaded on 11/12/2025 at 01:23:22 PM) [2025:RJ-JD:52298] (3 of 6)
[CSA-137/2025] 39 Rules 1 and 2 CPC on 03.06.2023 after addressing objections regarding maintainability.
The said order was reversed in appeal on 22.03.2024, prompting another writ petition (S.B. CWP No. 6299/2024), wherein this Court once again ordered maintenance of status quo.
Parallelly, an application under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC, filed by the defendants on 19.11.2022, was heard and decided

; the Trial Court, by order dated 17.12.2024, allowed the application and rejected the suit, holding it to be not maintainable and the order was affirmed in first appeal on 18.03.2025,
giving rise to the present second appeal.
3.
Learned counsel for the appellants assails the impugned judgments, contending that rejection of the plaint is vitiated by erroneous application of Order VII Rule 11 CPC.
It is urged that limitation is a mixed question of fact and law and could not have been decided at the threshold.

Reliance is placed on decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C. Natarajan, Dali Ben Valjibhai, and Geeta v.
Nanjudas Swami to contend that the plaint must be examined only on its own averments and not on disputed facts or defences.

It is submitted that the unregistered document relied upon by the appellants could not have been a ground to reject the suit at the preliminary stage, nor was the suit barred under the Specific Relief Act or the Land Acquisition Act.
On these premises, it is urged that the impugned orders suffer from perversity and disregard settled law.

sentences.text: Per contra, learned counsel for the respondents supports the concurrent findings and submits that no substantial question of (Uploaded on 11/12/2025 at 01:23:22 PM) [2025:RJ-JD:52298] (4 of 6) [CSA-137/2025] law arises under Section 100 CPC.

It is contended that the "ikararnama" relied upon by the appellants does not create any right, title or interest in immovable property and, at best,
contemplates a conditional arrangement dependent upon prior compliance by the appellants, which has neither been pleaded nor established.
Thus, the plaint was rightly rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, and the dismissal of the first appeal warrants no interference.
5. I have heard the counsel for the parties and gone through the impugned judgments of both the courts below and other material available on record.

6. After going through the impugned judgments, it is an admitted position that an agreement to sale was executed between the plaintiff and a private respondent and during the subsistence of this arrangement, the land in question came under acquisition.
Statutory notices were issued in the acquisition proceedings, and such notices were admittedly received by the said private respondent.
Upon culmination of the process, the land vested in the State and was subsequently placed at the disposal of RIICO.
Despite this, the plaintiff now seeks a direction compelling RIICO to execute a sale deed in his favour.
Such a claim is wholly misconceived.
There is not even a whisper of contractual privity between the plaintiff and RIICO.

The plaintiff does not possess a better title, nor does the agreement executed between the plaintiff and the private respondent contain any covenant binding a third (Uploaded on 11/12/2025 at 01:23:22 PM) [2025:RJ-JD:52298] (5 of 6)
[CSA-137/2025] party to step into the obligations arising from it.
The plea that RIICO stands "in the shoes" of the private respondent is entirely untenable.
At the highest, the plaintiff may pursue his monetary remedies against the private respondent, but no declaratory or injunctive relief can be claimed against RIICO.
The very nature of the relief sought renders the suit ousted by jurisdiction.
6.1 Once the acquisition machinery was set into motion, the plaintiff was at full liberty to intervene and assert his claim before the Land Acquisition Officer.

Having chosen not to avail such statutory remedies, he cannot subsequently maintain a suit seeking declaration and injunction to compel RIICO, a statutory corporation to execute a sale deed in his favour.
Courts cannot be invited to circumvent the statutory consequences of acquisition.
The suit was, therefore, rightly dismissed by the courts below.
The findings relating to acquisition of the land by RIICO also remain unimpeached.
Once land is acquired under statutory procedure and compensation is accepted, all antecedent rights stand extinguished.
Any money or arrangement concerning such land, outside the statutory framework, is void and incapable of conferring rights.
The suit, therefore, lacks a legally sustainable foundation.
6.2 This Court is mindful of the limited scope of interference under Section 100 CPC, which is confined to substantial questions of law.
The appellants have failed to demonstrate the existence of any such question.

The concurrent findings are factual, consistent (Uploaded on 11/12/2025 at 01:23:22 PM) [2025:RJ-JD:52298] (6 of 6) [CSA-137/2025] with statutory provisions and settled principles, and do not merit re-appreciation.
7. In view of the above, this Court finds itself in full agreement with the concurrent findings of the courts below.

The lower courts have undertaken a thorough and legally sound analysis of the Dalpat Singh vs Lrs Of Jabbar Singh on 5 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/146983264/
3 pleadings, the nature of relief sought, and the legal effect of the document forming the foundation of the suit.

sentences.text: No material has been placed before this Court to establish that the findings suffer from perversity, misdirection in law, or omission of relevant facts.
8. For the foregoing reasons, this Court finds no infirmity in the impugned judgments.
No substantial question of law arises for determination under Section 100 CPC.
The Civil Second Appeal, being devoid of merit, is accordingly dismissed.
No order as to costs.
9. The stay petition and all pending applications, if any stand disposed of.

10. Let the record be transmitted back to the court concern.
